description: The legislative process from first reading to royal assent, and the role of MPs at each stage.
content_html:
What Is a Bill?

Before a new law is passed, it begins life as a Bill. A Bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to existing law. Most Bills are introduced by the government (called government Bills), but MPs and Lords can also introduce Bills privately (called private members’ Bills). Once a Bill has passed through all the stages in Parliament and received royal assent, it becomes an Act of Parliament — a law. The legislative process has several distinct stages and ensures that proposed laws are scrutinised, debated and (where necessary) amended before they come into force.

The Stages of the Legislative Process

A Bill typically passes through both the House of Commons and the House of Lords, though some Bills begin in the Lords. Each House considers the Bill through five stages: First Reading, Second Reading, Committee Stage, Report Stage and Third Reading. After both Houses have agreed on the same text, the Bill is sent for royal assent.

First Reading is a formal announcement that the Bill has been introduced. The title is read out and the Bill is printed. No debate takes place at this stage. It is purely procedural.

Second Reading is the main debate on the general principles of the Bill. MPs or Lords debate whether the Bill’s broad aims are worthwhile and vote on whether it should proceed. If the Bill fails this vote, it falls. The Second Reading is the most politically significant early stage — whips work hard to ensure their party’s members vote the right way.

Committee Stage is where a small group of MPs (a Public Bill Committee, or the whole Commons for certain constitutional Bills) scrutinises the Bill line by line. They can propose and vote on amendments to specific clauses. This is where the detailed work of legislation is done. External experts or affected groups may give evidence to the committee.

Report Stage allows the full House to consider the amendments made in Committee Stage. Further amendments can be put forward and debated. All MPs have the opportunity to contribute, unlike the committee stage which involves only selected members.

Third Reading is the final debate in that House. It is usually brief. MPs vote on the Bill as amended. If it passes, the Bill moves to the other House (Lords or Commons) and goes through the same stages again. If both Houses pass different versions of the Bill, it goes back and forth in a process called ‘ping-pong’ until they agree on the same text.

Key Fact

The five stages a Bill passes through in each House are: First Reading (formal introduction, no debate), Second Reading (debate on general principles, first vote), Committee Stage (line-by-line scrutiny, amendments), Report Stage (full House considers amendments), Third Reading (final debate and vote). A Bill must pass through both Houses before receiving royal assent.

Royal Assent

Once both Houses have agreed on the same final text of a Bill, it is sent to the monarch for royal assent. Royal assent is given on the advice of the government. By constitutional convention, the monarch does not refuse royal assent — the last time a monarch refused was in 1707. Once royal assent is given, the Bill becomes an Act of Parliament and comes into force, either immediately or on a date specified in the Act itself.

If the House of Lords rejects or significantly amends a Bill, it is returned to the Commons — a process sometimes called ‘ping-pong.’ The Lords can delay a Bill by up to one parliamentary year. Under the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, if the Lords continue to block a Bill that has been passed by the Commons in two successive sessions, the Commons can pass the Bill without the Lords’ consent. This power is rarely used but exists as an important constitutional mechanism to prevent the unelected Lords from permanently blocking the will of the elected Commons. Finance Bills (relating to government taxation and spending) can only be delayed by the Lords for one month, giving the Commons much stronger control over financial legislation.

Key Fact

The role of MPs in the legislative process includes: debating the general principles of a Bill at Second Reading; scrutinising it line by line at Committee Stage and proposing amendments; considering further changes at Report Stage; and giving a final vote at Third Reading. MPs also represent constituents who may be affected by the proposed law, and may speak in debates to reflect local concerns or campaign interests.

Government Bills are introduced by ministers and are given priority parliamentary time. They form the bulk of legislation and usually reflect the governing party’s programme announced in the King’s Speech. Because the government controls the timetable, government Bills have a high success rate.

Private members’ Bills are introduced by backbench MPs or Lords. They are entered into a ballot and those drawn first get limited debating time on specific Fridays. Most private members’ Bills do not become law because they run out of parliamentary time, but some important laws began as private members’ Bills — for example, the Abortion Act 1967. A private Bill, by contrast, is different again: it deals with specific organisations or localities rather than the general public.

Why the Legislative Process Matters for Citizens

The staged legislative process exists to ensure that laws are considered carefully before they come into force. Each stage gives MPs, Lords and experts opportunities to identify problems, propose improvements and debate the implications for different groups. Citizens can engage with the process: by writing to their MP, giving evidence to a committee, petitioning Parliament, or joining campaigns that seek to influence a Bill’s content. Understanding how a Bill becomes law is fundamental to understanding how citizens can bring about political change through parliamentary channels.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark ‘Describe’ question about the legislative process, describe two stages in specific detail rather than listing five stages superficially. For example: “At Committee Stage, a small group of MPs scrutinises the Bill clause by clause and can propose amendments to specific sections. This is significant because it allows detailed improvements before the Bill returns to the full House.” That is worth 2 marks for one stage; add a second equally developed stage for full marks. A common mistake is giving a bare list of stage names — that scores only 1 mark per stage at most. For 8-mark ‘Analyse’ questions about the process, remember to weigh the strengths of scrutiny (multiple stages, expert input, Lords’ amendments) against limitations (government Bills usually pass because the governing party controls the timetable, limited time for private members’ Bills).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A Bill passes through five stages in each House (First Reading, Second Reading, Committee Stage, Report Stage, Third Reading) before receiving royal assent from the monarch and becoming an Act of Parliament.
  • MPs play key roles at each stage: debating principles at Second Reading, scrutinising details and proposing amendments at Committee Stage, and voting on the final text at Third Reading.
  • If the Lords reject a Bill, it can be delayed but not permanently blocked; under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the Commons can ultimately pass a Bill without the Lords’ consent after a period of delay.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the First Reading stage of a Bill?
A) A full debate on the general principles of the Bill with a vote
B) A line-by-line examination of the Bill by a small committee of MPs
C) A formal announcement introducing the Bill; no debate takes place
D) A final debate followed by a vote before the Bill is sent to the Lords
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) A formal announcement introducing the Bill; no debate takes place.

practice_questions.text: Identify two stages in the legislative process through which a Bill passes in the House of Commons.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two distinct named stages: First Reading / Second Reading / Committee Stage / Report Stage / Third Reading. Two versions of the same stage (e.g. 'committee' and 'Public Bill Committee') score 1 mark only. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which MPs can influence a Bill during the legislative process.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks; 2 marks per way. Example answers: (1) At Second Reading, MPs debate the general principles of the Bill and vote on whether it should proceed — a strong Second Reading debate can signal political problems the government needs to address. (2) At Committee Stage, MPs scrutinise the Bill clause by clause and can propose and vote on amendments to specific sections. (3) At Report Stage, all MPs can table further amendments and debate changes made in committee. (4) During Third Reading, MPs make a final vote on the Bill as amended, and back bench MPs from the governing party who rebel and vote against the Bill can threaten its passage. Evaluation is not required.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A backbench MP published a statement on their website in 2024 following the defeat of their private member's Bill on mandatory nutritional labelling: 'Despite overwhelming public support shown in our petition of 87,000 signatures, the Bill ran out of parliamentary time on its third Friday slot. The government declined to grant additional time. This shows clearly that Parliament's process favours the government and makes it very difficult for backbench MPs to legislate, however strong the public backing.'"

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does the source tell us about the legislative process for private members' Bills?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying a specific detail from the source (e.g. the Bill ran out of parliamentary time despite 87,000 petition signatures). 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (e.g. the legislative process gives the government control over the timetable, making it hard for backbench MPs to pass legislation without government support). 1 mark for applying own knowledge (e.g. private members' Bills get limited Friday debating slots via a ballot; the government controls the main timetable; in contrast, government Bills are given priority and most become law). 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. weighing whether the current process is sufficiently democratic given the difficulty for backbenchers, or noting that some important laws — such as the Abortion Act 1967 — did originate as private members' Bills). Pure summary of the source caps at 1-2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse whether the legislative process in the UK Parliament effectively scrutinises proposed laws before they come into force.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Presents a well-developed two-sided analysis weighing the strengths of the legislative process (multiple stages, expert committee input, Lords' ability to amend and delay, independent scrutiny at Report Stage) against limitations (government control of timetable, government Bills usually pass with large majorities, limited time for private members' Bills). Names real-world examples (Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949; select committee evidence-taking; use of ping-pong). Uses accurate vocabulary. Reaches a clear substantiated judgement.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides present, at least one named example, generally accurate, some analytical development.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant content but one-sided or both sides underdeveloped. Limited named reference.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic description of one or two stages. Little or no named example. Descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text:
'The House of Lords plays an essential role in the UK's legislative process.'

Evaluate this statement. In your answer consider arguments for and against, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A sustained two-sided evaluation naming real-world examples on each side. For: the Lords scrutinises Bills in detail, proposes amendments that improve legislation, delays controversial measures to allow reconsideration, and brings expert knowledge (e.g. life peers with medical, legal or scientific expertise). Against: the Lords is unelected and therefore lacks democratic mandate; the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 limit its power to delay; its composition (largely appointed on government advice) raises questions about independence. Reaches a clear substantiated overall judgement. Deploys accurate vocabulary (bicameral, royal assent, ping-pong, Parliament Acts, private members' Bills).

Secure (7-9 marks): Both viewpoints addressed. At least one named example. A judgement is reached.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some two-sided content. Limited development or examples. Judgement may be weak.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of the Lords' role. Little or no real-world reference. No meaningful judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: At which stage of the legislative process do MPs scrutinise a Bill clause by clause and propose amendments?
What happens when the monarch gives 'royal assent' to a Bill?
options: The Bill is sent back to the Lords for further debate
The Bill formally becomes an Act of Parliament — a law
The Bill is rejected and must be reintroduced
The Bill is referred to the Supreme Court for review

knowledge_checks.q: A proposal for a new law introduced in Parliament is called a _____; it only becomes an Act of Parliament after receiving royal assent.
The _____ stage is the main debate on a Bill's general principles, at which MPs vote on whether the Bill should proceed.
Match each stage of the legislative process to what happens at that stage:
right: Main debate on the Bill's general principles; first vote on whether it should proceed
Line-by-line scrutiny of the Bill by a small group of MPs; amendments can be proposed
Formal approval by the monarch, after which the Bill becomes an Act of Parliament

flashcard_questions.q: What is a Bill in the context of Parliament?
flashcard_questions.a: A draft proposed law debated and voted on before it can become an Act of Parliament.
The Bill is formally introduced; no debate takes place.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of Second Reading?
flashcard_questions.a: A full debate on the Bill's general principles, followed by a vote on whether it should proceed.
A small group of MPs scrutinises the Bill clause by clause and can propose amendments.
The full House considers amendments made at Committee Stage and can propose further changes.
The final debate and vote in that House on the Bill as amended.
Formal approval by the monarch; the Bill becomes an Act of Parliament.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'ping-pong' in the legislative process?
flashcard_questions.a: When a Bill passes back and forth between Commons and Lords until both agree on the same text.
A Bill introduced by ministers and given priority parliamentary time; most become law.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a private member's Bill?
flashcard_questions.a: A Bill introduced by a backbench MP or Lord; most fail due to limited parliamentary time.

flashcard_questions.q: Under the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, what can the Commons do if the Lords repeatedly rejects a Bill?
flashcard_questions.a: Pass the Bill without the Lords' consent after a period of delay.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Act of Parliament began as a private member's Bill?

glossary_terms.definition: A draft piece of legislation that is debated and voted on by Parliament before it can become an Act of Parliament (a law).
A Bill that has passed all stages in Parliament and received royal assent, making it a law of the land.
The formal approval of a Bill by the monarch, after which it becomes an Act of Parliament and has the force of law.
Bills introduced by the government and given parliamentary time by the government; the most common and most likely to become law.
Bills introduced by an MP or Lord who is not a government minister; most are unlikely to become law unless they gain government support.
The stage of the legislative process in which a small group of MPs scrutinises a Bill clause by clause, proposing and voting on detailed amendments before it returns to the full House.
